name: Geoffrey Huntley
role: Engineer and writer who created the 'Ralph Wiggum' agent loop technique.

sources.title: The Ralph Playbook (Clayton Farr; fork at ghuntley/how-to-ralph-wiggum)

philosophy: Software is built as a loop, not brick by brick: a bash while-loop that feeds the same prompt to a fresh agent context, one task per iteration, with tests and type checks as backpressure. Watch the loop and tune the prompt whenever it fails.
process: Talk through the idea and write one spec per topic in specs/*.md
Planning prompt: have Ralph study the specs and the source and create or update a prioritised @fix_plan.md, then switch from planning to building mode
Building loop: while :; do cat PROMPT.md | <agent> ; done, picking the single most important item per iteration
Main context acts as scheduler; subagents search and summarise (many in parallel) but only one runs build/test
Backpressure: tests, type checkers and static analysis; no placeholders; commit and tag when green
Watch the stream; when it misbehaves, tune the prompt (add a 'sign') and let Ralph keep @AGENT.md up to date, or git reset --hard and start the loop again
Prefer greenfield projects
tools: type checkers / static analysers (e.g. Pyrefly, Dialyzer)

name: Matt Pocock
role: TypeScript educator (Total TypeScript, AI Hero), author of the 'Skills For Real Engineers' repo.

sources.title: 5 agent skills I use every day (AI Hero)

philosophy: Small, composable, model-agnostic skills that keep you in control (unlike frameworks that own the process). Align with the agent first by being grilled on the plan, build a shared domain language, and rely on tight feedback loops.
process: Run /setup-matt-pocock-skills once per repo (issue tracker, triage labels, docs location)
Align: /grill-with-docs for code changes (also maintains GLOSSARY.md and ADRs); /grill-me for non-code plans
/to-spec: turn the conversation into a spec published to the issue tracker
/to-tickets: split it into vertical-slice tickets with blocking edges
/implement with /tdd red-green-refactor (/diagnosing-bugs for hard bugs)
/code-review against standards and the spec
/improve-codebase-architecture weekly or after a burst of work; /handoff to pass context to another agent
tools: issue tracker of choice (GitHub, GitLab or local files)
static types, browser access and automated tests as feedback loops

name: Mitchell Hashimoto
role: Co-founder of HashiCorp; creator of Ghostty terminal
philosophy: Use real agents, not chat. Get good at them by redoing your own work, and when an agent makes a mistake, fix the harness (AGENTS.md, scripts) so it does not happen again. Never ship AI code you don't understand or haven't reviewed.
process: Split work into clear tasks; separate planning sessions from execution sessions
Plan with a slow read-only 'oracle' model and save the plan as a spec file
Give agents ways to verify themselves (filtered test scripts, screenshot scripts)
Use the last 30 minutes of the day for background agents (research, exploration, issue triage that only writes reports)
Each morning hand off sure-win tasks to a single background agent; turn agent notifications off
When an agent repeats a mistake, update AGENTS.md (per-directory) or add a tool
Review everything manually before merging; rewrite parts by hand when needed

Run 3-8 agents in parallel in a terminal grid (Oct 2025: mostly on main without worktrees; his current AGENTS.MD says to create task-owned git worktrees whenever useful)
Iterate with screenshots and short prompts; queue 'continue' messages for long tasks
Have the model write tests in the same context after each feature
Agents commit only their own files ('commit/push'); land PRs with /landpr-style prompts
Keep a global AGENTS.md updated whenever something goes wrong

name: Simon Willison
role: Independent developer and blogger, co-creator of Django, creator of Datasette and the llm CLI.

sources.title: Embracing the parallel coding agent lifestyle
Claude Skills are awesome, maybe a bigger deal than MCP
Introducing Showboat and Rodney, so agents can demo what they've built
A new way to extract detailed transcripts from Claude Code

philosophy: Agentic engineering means professionals amplifying their expertise with agents. Code is cheap now, so spend effort on tests, proof that the code works, and safe sandboxes. Prefer CLI tools and skills over MCP.
process: Open each session with 'First run the tests' (for example uv run pytest) so the agent knows the suite exists
Implement with 'Use red/green TDD'
Have the agent prove the feature by hand-testing it and recording a demo (showboat, with rodney for browser screenshots)
Understand unfamiliar code through linear walkthroughs and interactive explanations
Run agents in parallel for research, scouting attempts, small maintenance and carefully specified tasks, each in a fresh checkout

Prefer YOLO mode in a sandbox or on someone else's computer (Docker, Codespaces, Codex Cloud, Claude Code for web) with test/staging credentials and a tight budget; he admits he also runs it locally when he is confident no malicious instructions can reach the context
Review the code before sharing it, and optionally publish the session transcript with claude-code-transcripts (he links transcripts from his commits)

name: Steve Yegge
role: Ex-Amazon/Google/Sourcegraph engineer; author of Beads (agent issue tracker) and Gas Town (multi-agent orchestrator)

sources.title: Introducing Beads: A Coding Agent Memory System

philosophy: Agents forget between sessions, and markdown TODO plans rot. Give them a dependency-aware issue graph they query for ready work and update as they go, and scale by orchestrating many agents (Gas Town).
process: Install bd once and run bd init per repo (writes AGENTS.md section and agent hooks)
bd prime is injected at SessionStart/PreCompact to restore workflow context
Agent runs bd ready to pick unblocked work and claims it (bd update <id> --claim)
File newly discovered work as issues with dependencies (bd create, bd dep add) instead of markdown TODOs
Close issues and store durable facts (bd close, bd remember) before ending the session
Scale to many parallel agents with Gas Town (gt)

name: Thorsten Ball
role: Co-creator of Amp (coding agent), previously at Sourcegraph and Zed; author of 'Writing an Interpreter in Go' and 'How to Build an Agent'

sources.title: Think Harder: How I Prompt (Laracon US talk)

philosophy: An agent is 'an LLM, a loop, and enough tokens' (an LLM with access to tools). Treat each prompt as a briefing: how is the model supposed to know what I mean? Move the 'how to do things' into the codebase (AGENTS.md files). He currently uses no MCP servers or custom slash commands.
process: You make the architecture decisions; the prompt spells out files, commits and constraints ('paint by numbers')
Two-step prompt: first have the agent find/load context, then make the request
Attach screenshots generously; give the agent visual feedback (Playwright/Storybook)
Start new threads often (quality drops beyond ~100k tokens)
Stage good changes in git, discard the rest; ask the agent to review its own diff
Put AGENTS.md files throughout the codebase; review load-bearing code closely

settings.notes: As of the Laracon US talk (2026-07-29) he uses no MCP servers, no custom slash commands, and only one or two skills, and builds custom tools as Amp plugins. He gives the agent a 'super long leash' and documents wherever it fails. In 2025 he used the Playwright and postgres MCP servers (How I Use Amp, now archived).
